definition: The maximum number of tokens a model can attend to at once when generating or processing text.
details: The context window bounds the prompt plus generated output a model can handle in a single pass. Performance is not uniform across the window: models often best use information at the very beginning or end of long contexts and can “lose” facts placed in the middle, a finding emphasized in the “lost in the middle” study.
story: Picture an architect laying out a building where every room has to know which other rooms matter to it. Think of it this way: The maximum number of tokens a model can attend to at once when generating or processing text. And here is the clever part: The context window bounds the prompt plus generated output a model can handle in a single pass. It is the difference between a row of isolated cubicles and one big room where everyone can hear each other. And that shape of the machine — Context Window — is what makes everything else possible.

citation.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
citation.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
